SeriesLinearAlgAccessor::inverse¶

Back to SeriesLinearAlgAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

Series SeriesLinearAlgAccessor::inverse() const
Series SeriesLinearAlgProxy::inverse() const

What It Does¶

inverse() computes the multiplicative inverse of each square matrix. If B = A.inverse(), then

A B = I    and    B A = I

up to floating-point rounding. The result has the same shape as the input. Every matrix in a batch is inverted independently.

Undoing A Linear Transformation¶

A matrix represents a linear transformation. Its inverse undoes that transformation: directions stretched by A are contracted by A^-1, and directions mixed by A are separated again.

An inverse exists only when the transformation preserves every independent direction. If rows or columns are dependent, information has been collapsed and no matrix can reconstruct it. That is why singular input is an error for inverse(), while det() can simply return zero.

In numerical code, forming an inverse is appropriate when the inverse itself is the desired result or will be reused as a matrix. If the actual goal is to solve a linear system, a solve method states that goal more directly and can avoid materializing the full inverse.

Shape Contract¶

Input shape

Interpretation

Output shape

[n, n]

one square matrix

[n, n]

[b, n, n]

b independent matrices

[b, n, n]

[..., n, n]

matrices indexed by leading dimensions

[..., n, n]

The final two dimensions must form square matrices. Leading dimensions are preserved exactly; there is no cross-batch interaction.

Returns¶

Series The inverse matrix or batch of inverse matrices, with the same shape as the input and floating-point values.

Gradient¶

If Y = A^-1 and the incoming matrix sensitivity is G = dL/dY, reverse mode uses

dL/dA = -A^-T G A^-T

The negative sign expresses an important fact: increasing A in a direction that strengthens the forward transformation generally weakens its inverse. For batched matrices, the formula is evaluated independently at every batch coordinate.

Examples¶

Example 1. Invert a two-by-two matrix.

auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 7.0}, {2.0, 6.0}});
std::cout << matrix.linearalg.inverse() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.6, -0.7],
  [-0.2, 0.4]]

Example 2. Multiplying by the inverse reconstructs the identity. Tiny residuals around zero are ordinary floating-point rounding.

auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 7.0}, {2.0, 6.0}});
auto inverse = matrix.linearalg.inverse();

std::cout << matrix.linearalg.mm(inverse) << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, -1.110223e-16],
  [1.110223e-16, 1]]

Example 3. Batch dimensions are retained and each matrix receives its own inverse.

auto batch = pluss::make_series({
    {{2.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 4.0}},
    {{1.0, 1.0}, {0.0, 2.0}},
});

std::cout << batch.linearalg.inverse() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2,2], strides=[4,2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=8, contiguous=true)
data=[[[0.5, -0],
  [0, 0.25]],
  [[1, -0.5],
  [0, 0.5]]]

Example 4. The gradient depends on both sides of the incoming sensitivity. Summing the inverse makes G a matrix of ones.

auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{2.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 4.0}});
matrix.tracks_slope_(true);

matrix.linearalg.inverse().sum().reverse();

std::cout << matrix.sensitivity() << "\n";

Because A^-T = diag(1/2, 1/4), the outer scaling of the all-ones sensitivity produces the four negative entries below.

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[-0.25, -0.125],
  [-0.125, -0.0625]]

Example 5. A singular matrix cannot be inverted.

try {
  auto singular = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {2.0, 4.0}});
  std::cout << singular.linearalg.inverse() << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::cout << e.what() << "\n";
}

Output¶

subsp::math::linalg::inverse: LU factorization failed

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Input must have at least two dimensions, and its final two dimensions must be square.

  • Every matrix in a batch must be invertible. One singular member makes the batched operation fail.

  • Near-singular matrices may produce very large inverse entries and magnify floating-point error even when factorization succeeds.

  • Identity checks should use a tolerance; exact zero residuals are not guaranteed by floating-point arithmetic.

Summary¶

inverse() returns the matrix that undoes each input transformation. It preserves all dimensions, supports independent matrix batches, and rejects singular matrices whose lost directions cannot be recovered.
